claims.claim: Reviewers report that the background and foreground visuals can be indistinguishable, making platforming frustrating.

citations.review_text:
This is in a weird spot for me. Were there a no thumbs up option, I would give this that. It is incredibly beautiful, with wonderful art direction and music and sound design. However, the game itself doesn't ever really come together for me personally.

In a weird way, this game most reminds me of Dark Souls. You travel silently through a sullen world marked by loss, progressing through ruins to discover their secrets. Though by the end of that analogy it's a bit tortured, I do think it aligns, and I don't think this game comes out the better in comparison.

There is a lack of progress to this - I genuinely have no idea how far I've gotten, how far there is to go, and so it feels eternal. I'm honestly shocked at how little I've played this, it feels like I've played for hours and hours. In Dark Souls, you can see the castles you are ascending - see further locations you go to both above and below, can see where you've come from, etc. I think this game would've benefited from that sort of visual progress.

Other than that it's a 2d side scroller, where you discover additional gameplay mechanics as the game goes on such as different jumps, heavy mode, etc. The gameplay feels very dated and juvenile compared to the rest of the work, which is so high effort I can't in good conscience give this a thumbs down.

I think if you are a little less curmudgeonly than I, you will like this. I think I would prefer this as a short animated series, rather than a game.

First the positives: aesthetic, sound, and vibe i guess.

But for me thats it. In Game you spend most of the time just walking. The puzzles are either really obvious or just unintuitive. Background and Foreground are often indistinguishable which makes the Jump n Run - or Jump n Walk in this case - quite frustrating.

I guess if you like artsy simple games with vague stories, it could be for you. For me it was just boring

cohorts.summary: Players experience a wordless story of puzzle platforming, while noting that technical issues require specific framerate adjustments.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that uncapped framerates cause physical and technical bugs, such as controls locking up during a specific encounter with a screaming bird or cutscenes getting stuck, which require capping the game at 60 FPS or changing monitor refresh rates to resolve.

citations.review_text: changing monitors frame rate to 60hz every cutscene so it doesnt get bugged is quite annoying

Beautiful. Bug at the crow requiring me to switch refresh rate to 60 was a little annoying, but I have no other problems with the game at all. It is exactly what it wants to be
EDIT: Honestly, having played a bit more, I'm finding myself just not having fun. I'm still leaving it a positive review because it might just not be my type of game and it's absolutely beautiful, but I'm just not really having an actively good time playing this.

GRIS is one of those rare games that reminds you that a masterpiece doesn't need a single line of dialogue to tell an unforgettable story. Every emotion is conveyed through breathtaking visuals, music, and atmosphere, making the journey deeply personal and incredibly moving. I did run into a couple of minor technical hiccups, like occasional frame stutters and cutscenes getting stuck, but that turned out to be because I had my FPS uncapped. Limiting it to 60 FPS fixed everything, and from that point on the experience was flawless. This is the kind of game that stays with you long after the credits roll. It is a beautiful reminder that games are an art form capable of telling powerful stories without ever saying a word.

I was honestly having a decent time with Gris until I ran into a completely game-breaking bug that killed the experience.

During the section where the giant bird screams at you, my controls completely locked up. You are supposed to use the "stone form" to block the wind, but the game refused to register a single input. I restarted multiple times, but I was softlocked every single time, unable to do anything while this bird just continuously screamed at my screen.

After doing some research, I found out this is a widely known issue. Apparently, the game's physics break at higher framerates, and the only way past it is to hard-cap the game at 60 FPS. The kicker is, Gris has incredibly bare-bones graphic settings and zero built-in options for an FPS lock. You have to go out of your way to force a limit through your GPU control panel just to progress.

It is frankly embarrassing that a major, progression-blocking bug like this still exists years after the game's release. No matter how pretty a game is, it doesn't excuse being unplayable. Cannot recommend.

I don't remember when I bought this game, but i've slept on it for so long. Feels like watching a very artistic short film, minimalistic, vibrant and beautiful. I originally thought that the was mostly a walking sim, however I was pleasantly surprised. The platforming mechanics in this game is very creative and level design complements it nicely. The levels become more and more complex as you progress and feels satisfying to complete. The soundtrack is soothing, calming and peaceful. Makes it all the more easier to admire the world of Gris. There is no dialogue and the story is abstract, leaving the story up for interpretation. Short game, but it feels like the right length.

The game is very good, however I did encounter a game breaking bug. If you have above 60fps you will be stuck on this section where a black raven comes down and screams at you. In 60fps you are supposed to be blown backwards. To fix this, close your game, change your refresh rate to 60hz and relaunch. Once you get blown back from the yell, you can set your refresh rate back.

[b][h2]8.7/10[/h2][/b]

Genuinely one of the most beautiful experiences I've ever had in a video game. The art style, the music, and the way the world slowly brings colour back in... it's just stunning. It feels less like playing a game and more like walking through a living piece of art. An absolute master piece. There were some really obnoxious bugs to do with refresh rate cap but besides that 10/10.

Right click on GRIS > Properties > General and right down below on Launch Options, paste or type this exactly as you see it: -window-mode exclusive

[h1] A Bit Basic, but Very Beautiful [/h1] 

Gris is a minimalistic metroidvania-lite 2D platformer that combines simple jumping and puzzle-solving with a melancholy atmosphere and some truly lovely visuals to create a soothing, calming, eye-pleasing experience, similar to a New Age guided meditation about Overcoming Grief through Inner Strength.
The game is stylistically closest to Journey and Ori and the Blind Forest, with a similar textless narrative and sincere, somewhat po-faced tone of etherial beauty and melancholy. If you enjoyed either of those games, Gris will probably align a similar chakra. 

Platforming is enjoyable, but rather easy. This is not a game that's out to challenge your fingers. Rather, you're best off relaxing and letting the gorgeous visuals and ambient music wash over you like an art degree bubble bath. There is some nice thematic stuff about overcoming sadness and finding the strength to go on in the face of grief to mull over and meditate upon as you play, but it is very general and non-specific, equally applicable to a friend not liking your Instagram post or a bad case of period cramps as it would be to a genuine traumatic loss. The game works best as a warm, comforting, soothing bit of digital self-care. I feel like this would make a middle-class teenage girl cry a lot.

I liked it a lot.

Indie games always and indeed forever are meant to be those titles that bring us the genuine feel, enjoyment, and raw emotion every gamer looks for—leaving a lasting impression that stays with you long after the credits roll. GRIS is the absolute definition of that philosophy, standing as a masterclass in visual and emotional storytelling.

From the very first moment, the game draws you into a breathtaking, watercolor world that feels like a living painting. Without using a single word of dialogue, it manages to convey a deeply moving journey through grief, restoration, and growth. The stunning hand-drawn art style, combined with an evocative and powerful musical score, creates an atmospheric experience that constantly sparks awe and wonder.

The gameplay stays delightfully simple, focusing on light platforming and intuitive puzzles that flow seamlessly into the narrative rather than getting in the way of it. It’s a peaceful, mesmerizing journey that respects your time and leaves you with an incredible sense of fulfillment once completed. If you appreciate games as a form of pure art, this is an absolute must-play.

Score: 9.5/10

Story: 10/10, despite not a single word being spoken.
Art: 10/10, every frame is like a painting.
Gameplay: It's not very complex, but it's exactly what it needed to be to let the other parts shine. 10/10.

I don’t think I can fully explain how much this game means to me. I’ve played it on multiple platforms, borrowed a friend’s Switch just to play it again, streamed it for my mom, made my best friend play it, watched countless other people experience it for the first time, and bought it for probably six or seven people at this point. I even have Gris tattooed on me.

There’s just something incredibly human about this game. Grief and loss are things we all experience eventually, and Gris manages to tell that story without needing to say a single word. The music, the art, the way the world changes as she moves through different stages of grief—it all communicates something that I think people can understand even if they don’t know anything about the game going into it.

I especially love that the stages of grief aren’t completely separate from one another. They overlap and bleed into each other, because that’s how grief actually feels. It isn’t a straight line.

I still listen to the soundtrack. I still cry every time I play. I still love watching other people experience it for the first time because I want to know what it makes them feel.

I’ve recommended a lot of games in my life, but this is the only one I’ve repeatedly bought for people just because I genuinely believe it’s worth experiencing.

If you decide to play Gris, maybe keep some tissues nearby.

[u][b]-Quick Review-[/b][/u]
Gris is a beautiful artistic 2d platformer indie game developed by Nomada Studio and released in 2018, where you play as a lost girl named Gris who is dealing with a painful experience in her life. The story description is left vague because there’s no dialogue of any kind and the story is told with music and imagery.

[u][b]Review Video:[/b][/u]
If you don't like reading, or are curious about watching gameplay check out my video here:
https://youtu.be/LG93A0-dGCI

[u][b]-Detailed breakdown review-[/b][/u]
[b]Story:[/b] As has already been said, the story for Gris is told without dialogue, without narration, without text. Another strength of this style of storytelling in this way is that it becomes universally accessible regardless of your spoken language.
Gris (the lost girl) has had her world shattered by some traumatic life event. The visuals are obviously meant to be interpreted metaphorically. The Game starts with Gris being held in the hand of a crumbling statue, Gris attempts to sing but can no longer do so, at this point Gris falls with the crumbling statue and all the color in her world is lost. You’ll spend the next few hours helping Gris struggle her way through the trials and tribulations to bring color back to the world and empower Gris to get through the ordeal.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3701562967

[b]Gameplay:[/b] Gris is a 2d platformer, so the controls are super simple, movement is A and D or directional inputs if you’re using a controller, jump, stomp, and sing buttons. I think Gris is slightly better when played with a controller because the layout is more natural, however you can play Gris on several different platforms and it’s good with keyboard controls too… just use what you’ve got available.
One of my favorite parts of the game is how at the end of each chapter, a new color was added to the world as Gris gets a bit stronger. It’s a very powerful narrative tool and Gris…

citations.review_text:
Pretentious with no element of substance of fun.
Features:
[list]
[*] Endless variations of the same rocky wasteland/temple ruins/scaffolding to walk through
[*] Soundtrack. If you like it or not.
[*] Walking.
[*] Zero challenge. You may have to jump a bit and you may have to be precise about it but you will never die.
[*] More walking.
[*] A story. Sort of. It's mainly walking and no dialogue.
[*] A guaranteed lack of fun.
[*] Did I mention walking yet?
[/list]

For once I decided to look for a single player game I've been in the mood for some me time and picked a random game from my library that game was Gris.
The game's plot is relatively simple. You play as a girl named Gris who's parental figure has died. You are sucked into darkness and go thru the 5 stages of grief. The game doesn't explicitly tell you this but it gives you context clues thru gameplay and cutscenes.
The game play is pretty straightforward it's a 2D side scroller platformer with some easy to medium problem solving. This game will not test you you physically cannot die. But given that the game is more of an emotional piece it's perfectly fine and still fun to play with some collectibles in there for trophy chasers.
By the end of each stage you get a new color which is the perfect metaphor of going thru grief each level has their own unique colors and themes and the music is very calming. The art direction in this game is spectacular and one of the most beautiful games I have ever played.
Overall this was a very calming and atmospheric game and I'm very glad I got to play it. It sucks that I'll get no replay value but considering it's $15 price tag I can't complain. This is a perfect example of how video games are a true form of art. 8/10

[h2]A Beautiful, Emotional Masterpiece[/h2][b]Visually stunning and mechanically meaningful.[/b][*] [b]Art Style:[/b] Breathtaking, watercolor-like visuals that feel like a living painting.[*] [b]Dynamic Audio:[/b] The incredible soundtrack seamlessly shifts and adapts to the action on screen.[*] [b]Zero Frustration:[/b] A peaceful, few-hour experience with no combat, hazards, or ways to die.[hr][/hr][h2]The Mechanics of Grief[/h2][b]Emotional growth translated perfectly into gameplay.[/b]The game masterfully connects its visual progression to the stages of grief. You start in a monochrome world, but as you heal, you literally bring color back to the environment.[b]A subtle, linear Metroidvania.[/b]As you navigate the emotional landscape, you unlock new abilities. Gaining these powers makes you feel increasingly capable, strong, and in control of a world that initially felt overwhelming.[hr][/hr][h2]Final Verdict: Highly Recommended[/h2]If you want a short, impactful, and artistic journey that proves video games are art, play GRIS. It is an unforgettable emotional experience.
